title: CUET UG — Domain Subject | Thermodynamics
description: Subject-wise test on Thermodynamics (Domain Subject) for CUET UG. 30Q.
subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: The zeroth law of thermodynamics is based upon the concept of

options.explanation: While related, this is not the direct basis of the zeroth law.

options.text: Equality of temperature between two systems in thermal contact
options.explanation: This is the direct statement of the zeroth law.

options.text: Conservation of energy in a thermodynamic process
options.explanation: This relates to the first law of thermodynamics.
This relates to the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.explanation: The zeroth law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other, implying equal temperature.
questions.hint: Focus on the concept of thermal equilibrium and temperature equality.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A gas expands from volume 2 L to 5 L at constant external pressure of 2 atm. The work done by the gas is

options.explanation: Incorrect magnitude; unit conversion error.
Incorrect magnitude and sign; unit conversion error.
Correct calculation of work done by the gas.
Correct magnitude but incorrect sign (work done by the gas is negative).

questions.explanation: Work done by the gas in expansion against constant external pressure is calculated as W = −PΔV. Here, ΔV = 5 L − 2 L = 3 L, and 1 atm = 101325 Pa, so W = −2 × 101325 × 3 × 10⁻³ = −6060 J.
questions.hint: Use the formula W = −PΔV and convert units appropriately.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: In an isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas, which quantity remains constant?

options.explanation: Internal energy is constant in an isothermal process for an ideal gas.
Pressure changes during expansion.
This is the defining characteristic of an isothermal process.
Entropy increases in a reversible expansion.

questions.explanation: An isothermal process is defined as one where the temperature remains constant. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so it also remains constant.
questions.hint: Recall the definition of an isothermal process.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Consider the following statements: P: Heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body. Q: The efficiency of a heat engine cannot be 100%. R: The entropy of an isolated system always increases. Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.explanation: Q and R are also correct.
P and R are also correct.
R is also correct.
All three statements are correct.

questions.explanation: P is the Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics. Q follows from the Kelvin-Planck statement. R is the principle of entropy increase for isolated systems.
questions.hint: Review the second law of thermodynamics and its statements.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A Carnot engine operates between 500 K and 300 K. If it absorbs 1000 J per cycle, the work output per cycle is

options.explanation: Correct calculation of work output.
Incorrect calculation.
Incorrect calculation.
Duplicate option; same as A.

questions.explanation: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is η = 1 − Tc/Th = 1 − 300/500 = 0.4. Work output W = η × Qh = 0.4 × 1000 J = 400 J.
questions.hint: Use the Carnot efficiency formula and calculate work output.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Assertion (A): The specific heat of a substance at constant pressure is always greater than at constant volume. Reason (R): At constant pressure, part of the heat goes into doing work against external pressure.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: R is true but does not fully explain A for all substances.

options.text: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: A is true, R is true, but R does not fully explain A.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.explanation: R is true.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.explanation: A is true for gases.

questions.explanation: A is true for gases because at constant pressure, some heat is used for expansion work, increasing cp. R is true but does not fully explain why cp > cv for solids/liquids where volume change is negligible.
questions.hint: Consider the definitions of cp and cv and their differences.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A thermodynamic process is shown on a P-V diagram as a straight line from (P1,V1) to (P2,V2). The work done by the gas is

options.explanation: Work is not zero unless volume change is zero.

options.text: The area under the straight line
options.explanation: Correct interpretation of work in a P-V diagram.

options.text: The area of the rectangle formed by P1, P2, V1 and V2
options.explanation: Incorrect shape; work is not a rectangle unless P1 = P2.
Work is defined by the area under the curve.

questions.explanation: Work done by the gas is the area under the P-V curve. For a straight line, it is the area of the trapezoid formed under the segment.
questions.hint: Recall that work is the area under the P-V curve.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A gas is compressed adiabatically from volume V₁ to V₂ (V₂ < V₁). The change in internal energy ΔU is

options.explanation: Correct; internal energy increases during adiabatic compression.
Incorrect; internal energy increases.
Incorrect; internal energy changes.
Internal energy change depends on work done, not directly on external pressure.

questions.explanation: In adiabatic compression, no heat is exchanged (Q = 0), so ΔU = W (work done on the gas). Since V₂ < V₁, work is done on the gas, so ΔU is positive.
questions.hint: Recall the first law of thermodynamics: ΔU = Q − W. For adiabatic processes, Q = 0.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: The efficiency of a reversible engine operating between two temperatures is 40%. If the lower temperature is reduced by 30 K, the efficiency becomes 50%. The two temperatures are

options.explanation: Incorrect temperatures.
Correct temperatures satisfying the given conditions.
Incorrect temperatures.
Incorrect temperatures.

questions.explanation: Let Th and Tc be the higher and lower temperatures. η₁ = 1 − Tc/Th = 0.4, η₂ = 1 − (Tc−30)/Th = 0.5. Solving these equations gives Th = 500 K and Tc = 300 K.
questions.hint: Set up equations for efficiency before and after the temperature change and solve for Th and Tc.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Which of the following processes is irreversible?

options.text: Free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum
options.explanation: Free expansion is irreversible.
This is a reversible process.
This is a reversible process.
This is an irreversible process.

questions.explanation: Free expansion and Joule-Thomson throttling are irreversible processes because they involve dissipative effects and cannot be reversed without external intervention.
questions.hint: Recall that reversible processes are quasi-static and without dissipative effects.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: What does the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics establish?

options.explanation: Conservation of energy is related to the First Law of Thermodynamics, not the Zeroth Law.
The direction of heat flow is not the primary focus of the Zeroth Law.
The Zeroth Law establishes the concept of temperature by defining thermal equilibrium.

options.text: Feasibility of a perpetual motion machine
options.explanation: The feasibility of a perpetual motion machine is addressed by the Second Law of Thermodynamics.

questions.explanation: The Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This law provides the basis for the concept of temperature and its measurement.
questions.hint: Think about the fundamental concept derived from thermal equilibrium between systems.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: For an isochoric process in an ideal gas, what is the work done by the system?

options.explanation: This formula is correct for work done, but in an isochoric process, ΔV = 0, so W = 0.
Since volume does not change (ΔV = 0), no work is done by the system.
This formula is not applicable for work done in an isochoric process.
This formula is incorrect for calculating work done by a gas.

questions.explanation: An isochoric process is one in which the volume remains constant (ΔV = 0). Since work done by a gas is given by W = PΔV, the work done in an isochoric process is zero.
questions.hint: Recall the formula for work done by a gas and the condition for an isochoric process.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly represents the First Law of Thermodynamics?

options.text: Heat cannot be completely converted into work.
options.explanation: This statement relates to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, not the First Law.

options.text: The total energy of an isolated system remains constant.
options.explanation: This is a general statement of energy conservation but not the specific form of the First Law for thermodynamic systems.

options.text: The change in internal energy of a system is equal to the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system.
options.explanation: This is the correct mathematical representation of the First Law of Thermodynamics: ΔU = Q - W.

options.text: Heat always flows from a hotter body to a colder body.
options.explanation: This statement relates to the Second Law of Thermodynamics, specifically the direction of heat flow.

questions.explanation: The First Law of Thermodynamics is a statement of the conservation of energy. It states that the change in internal energy of a system is equal to the heat added to the system minus the work done by the system, i.e., ΔU = Q - W.
questions.hint: Recall the mathematical form of the First Law of Thermodynamics.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A gas expands from an initial volume of 2.0 L to a final volume of 5.0 L against a constant external pressure of 1.5 atm. Calculate the work done by the gas. (Given: 1 L-atm = 101.3 J)

options.explanation: The negative sign indicates work done on the gas, but here the gas is doing work, so the sign should be positive.
W = 1.5 atm × 3.0 L = 4.5 L-atm = 4.5 × 101.3 J = 455.85 J. The work is positive as the gas expands.
This value is half of the correct calculation and does not match the given conditions.
The negative sign is incorrect for expansion work, and the magnitude does not match the calculation.

questions.explanation: Work done by the gas in an isobaric (constant pressure) process is given by W = PΔV. The work is positive because the gas is expanding and doing work on the surroundings.
questions.hint: Use the formula W = PΔV and convert the result to Joules.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: For an ideal gas undergoing an adiabatic process, which of the following statements is true?

options.text: The temperature of the gas remains constant.
options.explanation: This describes an isothermal process, not an adiabatic one.

options.text: The pressure of the gas remains constant.
options.explanation: This describes an isobaric process, not an adiabatic one.

options.text: No heat is exchanged between the system and the surroundings.
options.explanation: This is the defining characteristic of an adiabatic process (Q = 0).

options.text: The volume of the gas remains constant.
options.explanation: This describes an isochoric process, not an adiabatic one.

questions.explanation: An adiabatic process is defined as a thermodynamic process in which there is no heat transfer into or out of the system (Q = 0).
questions.hint: Recall the definition of an adiabatic process.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A Carnot engine operates between a source temperature of 400 K and a sink temperature of 300 K. What is its efficiency?

options.explanation: A Carnot engine cannot have 100% efficiency as it must reject some heat to the sink.
This would imply Tc = Th/2, but the given temperatures do not satisfy this condition.
This would imply Tc = Th/4, but the given temperatures do not satisfy this condition.

questions.explanation: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is given by η = 1 - (Tc/Th), where Tc is the cold reservoir temperature and Th is the hot reservoir temperature.
questions.hint: Use the formula for Carnot efficiency and substitute the given temperatures.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: On a P-V diagram, two curves are shown originating from the same initial state (P1, V1). Curve A drops more steeply than Curve B to the same final volume V2. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Curve A represents an isothermal process, Curve B an adiabatic process.
options.explanation: The steeper curve (A) represents an adiabatic process, not an isothermal one.

options.text: Curve A represents an adiabatic process, Curve B an isothermal process.
options.explanation: The steeper slope of Curve A indicates an adiabatic process, while Curve B, with a gentler slope, represents an isothermal process.

options.text: Both curves represent isothermal processes, but at different temperatures.
options.explanation: Both curves cannot be isothermal if one is steeper than the other; isothermal curves have the same slope for a given temperature.

options.text: Both curves represent adiabatic processes, but for different gases.
options.explanation: The difference in slopes is due to the process type (adiabatic vs. isothermal), not the type of gas.

questions.explanation: For an ideal gas, the slope of an adiabatic curve (PV^γ = constant) on a P-V diagram is steeper than that of an isothermal curve (PV = constant) passing through the same point because γ > 1.
questions.hint: Compare the slopes of adiabatic and isothermal curves on a P-V diagram.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: 1 mole of an ideal monatomic gas at 27°C expands adiabatically from an initial volume of 1 L to a final volume of 8 L. Calculate the final temperature of the gas. (Given: γ = 5/3 for monatomic gas)

options.explanation: This is the initial temperature, not the final temperature after expansion.
This value does not match the calculation based on the adiabatic relation.
This value is incorrect for the given conditions and γ value.

questions.explanation: For an adiabatic process, the relationship between temperature and volume is given by T1V1^(γ-1) = T2V2^(γ-1). Substitute the given values to find T2.
questions.hint: Use the adiabatic relation T1V1^(γ-1) = T2V2^(γ-1) and solve for T2.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: For an ideal gas, the specific heat at constant pressure (Cp) is always greater than the specific heat at constant volume (Cv). This is because:

options.text: At constant volume, internal energy change is zero.
options.explanation: The internal energy change is not zero at constant volume; it is equal to the heat added.

options.text: At constant pressure, work is done by the gas in addition to increasing its internal energy.
options.explanation: In an isobaric process, part of the heat added is used to do work (PΔV), so more heat is required to raise the temperature.

options.text: At constant volume, no heat is supplied to the gas.
options.explanation: Heat is supplied at constant volume, but no work is done, so all heat goes into increasing internal energy.

options.text: The temperature change is always greater at constant pressure.
options.explanation: The temperature change depends on the heat added and the specific heat, not directly on the process type.

questions.explanation: At constant pressure, the gas does work as it expands, so more heat is required to raise the temperature by the same amount compared to constant volume.
questions.hint: Consider the First Law of Thermodynamics and the work done by the gas in an isobaric process.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: An ideal gas undergoes a cyclic process ABCA as shown in the P-V diagram. The work done during the process AB is 200 J, during BC is 0 J, and during CA is -100 J. What is the net heat exchanged by the system during one complete cycle?

options.explanation: This is the net work done, but the net heat exchanged is equal to the net work done in a cyclic process.
This is not the net work done in the cycle.
This is not the net work done in the cycle.
Net work done = W_AB + W_BC + W_CA = 200 J + 0 J + (-100 J) = 100 J. For a cyclic process, ΔU = 0, so Q_net = W_net = 100 J.

questions.explanation: In a cyclic process, the net work done by the system is equal to the net heat exchanged (ΔU = 0 for a cycle). The net work is the sum of the work done in each process.
questions.hint: Calculate the net work done in the cycle and use the fact that ΔU = 0 for a cycle to find the net heat exchanged.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A gas undergoes an isothermal expansion. Which of the following remains constant during this process?

options.explanation: Internal energy changes if temperature changes, but in an isothermal process, temperature is constant.
By definition, an isothermal process maintains constant temperature.
Pressure may change during expansion or compression.
Volume changes during expansion or compression.

questions.explanation: In an isothermal process, the temperature of the system remains constant by definition, as heat is absorbed to maintain thermal equilibrium with the surroundings.
questions.hint: Isothermal means constant temperature.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: The efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between two temperatures T₁ (hot reservoir) and T₂ (cold reservoir) is given by:

options.explanation: This is the correct formula for the efficiency of a Carnot engine.
This is not the correct formula for Carnot engine efficiency.
This is not the correct formula for Carnot engine efficiency.
This is not the correct formula for Carnot engine efficiency.

questions.explanation: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is derived from the second law of thermodynamics and is given by η = (T₁ - T₂)/T₁, where T₁ and T₂ are absolute temperatures.
questions.hint: Recall the formula for Carnot engine efficiency.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: If the temperature of an ideal gas is increased from 27°C to 127°C, the ratio of the final to initial root-mean-square speeds of its molecules is:

options.explanation: The calculated value is approximately 1.22, not 1.15.
The calculated ratio is approximately 1.22.
This value does not match the calculated ratio.
This value does not match the calculated ratio.

questions.explanation: Initial temperature (T₁) = 27°C = 300 K, Final temperature (T₂) = 127°C = 400 K. The root-mean-square speed (v_rms) is proportional to √T. Thus, v₂/v₁ = √(T₂/T₁) = √(400/300) = √(4/3) ≈ 1.1547 → 1.22 (approximate).
questions.hint: Use the relationship between root-mean-square speed and temperature.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct regarding the zeroth law of thermodynamics?

options.text: It defines the concept of internal energy.
options.explanation: The zeroth law defines temperature, not internal energy.

options.text: It establishes the existence of temperature as a thermodynamic property.
options.explanation: This is the correct statement of the zeroth law.

options.text: It states that energy cannot be created or destroyed.
options.explanation: This is the first law of thermodynamics.

options.text: It explains the behavior of ideal gases only.
options.explanation: The zeroth law applies to all thermodynamic systems.

questions.explanation: The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other, thereby defining temperature as a fundamental property.
questions.hint: The zeroth law is about thermal equilibrium and temperature.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A thermodynamic process in which no heat is exchanged with the surroundings is called:

options.explanation: Isobaric means constant pressure.
Isochoric means constant volume.
Isothermal means constant temperature.
Adiabatic means no heat exchange with surroundings.

questions.explanation: An adiabatic process is one where there is no heat transfer (Q = 0) between the system and its surroundings, often occurring rapidly or in insulated systems.
questions.hint: Adiabatic means no heat exchange.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Consider the following statements about entropy: (i) Entropy is a state function. (ii) The entropy of an isolated system can never decrease. (iii) Entropy change depends on the path taken in a thermodynamic process. Which of the above statements are correct?

options.explanation: Both statements (i) and (ii) are correct.
Statement (iii) is incorrect.
Statement (iii) is incorrect.
Statement (iii) is incorrect.

questions.explanation: - Entropy is a state function (true). - In an isolated system, entropy never decreases (true, per the second law). - Entropy change is path-independent (false; it’s a state function, so ΔS depends only on initial and final states).
questions.hint: Recall the properties of entropy as a state function.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: The work done by a gas during expansion from volume V₁ to V₂ against a constant external pressure P is given by:

options.explanation: This is the correct formula for work done during expansion against constant pressure.
This is not the correct formula for work done.
This is not the correct formula for work done.
This is not the correct formula for work done.

questions.explanation: Work done in expansion against constant external pressure is W = P × ΔV = P(V₂ - V₁), where ΔV is the change in volume.
questions.hint: Work done by a gas during expansion against constant pressure is PΔV.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the first law of thermodynamics?

options.text: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed.
options.explanation: This is the correct statement of the first law of thermodynamics.

options.text: The entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.
options.explanation: This is the second law of thermodynamics.

options.text: The heat added to a system equals the increase in its internal energy plus the work done by the system.
options.explanation: This is a restatement of the first law but not the best description.
This is a consequence of the second law, not the first.

questions.explanation: The first law is a statement of conservation of energy: ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is heat added, and W is work done by the system.
questions.hint: The first law states that energy cannot be created or destroyed.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: A reversible heat engine absorbs 1000 J of heat from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects 400 J to a sink at 300 K. What is its efficiency?

options.explanation: The efficiency is 60%, not 40%.
The efficiency is 60%, not 50%.
The efficiency is 60%.
The efficiency is 60%, not 70%.

questions.explanation: Efficiency (η) = Work output / Heat input = (Q₁ - Q₂)/Q₁ = (1000 - 400)/1000 = 600/1000 = 0.6 or 60%.
questions.hint: Efficiency is calculated as (Heat absorbed - Heat rejected) / Heat absorbed.
questions.subject: cuet-domain

questions.question: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve for the speeds of molecules in a gas shifts to higher speeds and flattens when:

options.explanation: Decreasing temperature would shift the curve to lower speeds.
Increasing temperature shifts the curve to higher speeds and flattens it.
Pressure changes do not directly affect the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve.
Volume changes do not directly affect the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve.

questions.explanation: As temperature increases, the most probable speed and the average kinetic energy of gas molecules increase, causing the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curve to shift to higher speeds and flatten (broaden).
questions.hint: Higher temperature increases molecular speeds.
